texts.label: text
texts.orig: Abstract  -  For a  long time, relational database management systems  have  been  the  only  solution  for  persistent  data  storage. However,  with  the  phenomenal  growth  of  data,  this  conventional way of storing has become problematic. To manage the exponentially growing data volumes, the largest information technology companies, such as Google and Amazon, have developed alternative solutions that store data in what have come to be known as NoSQL databases. Some of the NoSQL features are flexible schema, horizontal scaling and relaxed consistency. NoSQL databases store and  replicate  data  in  distributed  systems, thereby achieving scalability and high availability. In this paper two NoSQL databases are reviewed and compared:  Amazon's Dynamo and Google's BigTable.

texts.orig: 1. INTRODUCTION
texts.text: 1. INTRODUCTION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the recent decade, new kind of databases, often referred to as NoSQL [1], had become popular. The main characteristic of these databases is a fact that they are not relational. Rather than  store  data  in  heavily  structured  tables,  NoSQL  systems prefer simpler data schema such as key-value pairs or collections  of  documents.  They  store  and  replicate  data  in distributed  systems,  commonly  across  datacenters,  by  which means  achieving  scalability  and  high  availability.  Most  of today's NoSQL databases are open source; nonetheless, many of  them  have  been  inspired  by  two  closed  source  systems -Amazon's Dynamo [2] and Google's BigTable [3].

texts.orig: B. BigTable
texts.text: B. BigTable

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Just  like  Amazon  built  Dynamo  for  their  internal  use, Google developed BigTable -a distributed storage system for managing structured data. It is designed to scale to a very large size  and  to  satisfy  the  needs  of  most  Google  applications. Unlike Dynamo's, BigTable's designers decided that key-value pair model is too limiting and chose a more sophisticated and flexible data model -multidimensional sorted map.
texts.text: Just  like  Amazon  built  Dynamo  for  their  internal  use, Google developed BigTable -a distributed storage system for managing structured data. It is designed to scale to a very large size  and  to  satisfy  the  needs  of  most  Google  applications. Unlike Dynamo's, BigTable's designers decided that key-value pair model is too limiting and chose a more sophisticated and flexible data model -multidimensional sorted map.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: BigTable uses Google File System (GFS) [6] as a storage platform.  GFS is a  scalable  and  fault  tolerant  distributed  file system, which works with huge files (by traditional standards). To  achieve  reliability  and  availability,  files  are  divided  into chunks, and each chunk is replicated across multiple machines.

To  achieve  reliability  and  availability,  files  are  divided  into chunks, and each chunk is replicated across multiple machines.

texts.orig: D. Partitioning
texts.text: D. Partitioning

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Dynamo  and  BigTable  are  highly  scalable  systems.  It means  that  they  can  adjust  themselves  to  the  changing  data volume by simply adding or removing nodes. This requires a mechanism to dynamically partition data over the nodes in the system,  and  Dynamo  and  BigTable  do  it  in  very  different ways.
texts.text: Dynamo  and  BigTable  are  highly  scalable  systems.  It means  that  they  can  adjust  themselves  to  the  changing  data volume by simply adding or removing nodes. This requires a mechanism to dynamically partition data over the nodes in the system,  and  Dynamo  and  BigTable  do  it  in  very  different ways.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Dynamo uses a technique called consistent hashing , where every node in the system is assigned to one or more points on a fixed circular space called 'ring' . Each data item, identified by a key, is assigned to a node by hashing its key with a hash function, whose output is a point on the ring, and then walking the  ring  clockwise  to  find  the  first  node  that  appears  on  it ( coordinator node).  The  main  advantage  of  this  technique  is that addition or removal of a node only affects its immediate neighbors and other nodes remain unaffected.

The  main  advantage  of  this  technique  is that addition or removal of a node only affects its immediate neighbors and other nodes remain unaffected.

texts.orig: E. Replication
texts.text: E. Replication

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To achieve high availability, reliability and durability, both systems replicate data on multiple hosts. However the techniques which are used by them are extremely different.
texts.text: To achieve high availability, reliability and durability, both systems replicate data on multiple hosts. However the techniques which are used by them are extremely different.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Dynamo replicates each data object at N nodes, where N is a user-defined parameter. As described in the previous section, each key K is assigned to a coordinator node. This node stores the data associated with K locally, and also replicates it at the N-1 healthy clockwise successor nodes in the ring.

texts.orig: In BigTable each table's cell belongs to a particular tablet, and  each  tablet  is  stored  in  GFS  as  a  sequence  of  read-only files  called  SSTables.  In  GFS,  SSTables  are  divided  into fixed-size chunks , and these chunks are stored on chunkservers . System architecture of GFS resembles BigTable's -a single master, which maintains system metadata and multiple chunkservers which are responsible for the data operations. Just like tablet servers in BigTable serve set  of  tablets,  chunkservers  in  GFS  serve  set  of  chunks.  An important  difference  between  these  two  systems  is  that  each tablet in BigTable  belongs  to exactly one  tablet server, whereas  each  chunk  in  GFS  is  replicated  across  multiple chunkservers (three by default, but can be configured).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: F. Storage
texts.text: F. Storage

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Each node in Dynamo has a local persistence engine where data  items  are  stored  as  binary  objects  (i.e.  blob).  Different Dynamo  instances  may  use  different  persistence  engines. Examples  of  the  engines  that  can  be  plugged-in  include MySQL and Berkeley Database (BDB). The main reason for designing a pluggable persistence component is to allow users to  choose  the  storage  engine  best  suited  for  their needs.  For instance, BDB handles relatively small objects (typically tens of  kilobytes)  whereas  MySQL  can  handle  objects  of  much larger sizes. Applications choose the persistence engine based on their object size distribution.

texts.orig: G. Read/Write Implementation
texts.text: G. Read/Write Implementation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To read and write replicated data, Dynamo uses a protocol similar  to  those  used  in  quorum  systems.  This  protocol  has two parameters R / W -the minimal number of nodes that must participate  in  a  successful read/write operation  respectively. When a coordinator receives  a  write  operation,  it  writes  the data  locally  and  then  sends  a  write  request  to  the  other  N-1 replica nodes. If at least W-1 nodes respond, the operation is considered successful and the coordinator informs the client. When  a  read  operation  is  received,  the  coordinator  sends  a read  request  to  the  N-1  nodes,  and  if  at  least  R-1  nodes respond, it returns the result to the client. If different objects are  received  from  different  nodes,  then  coordinator  sends  to the  client  a  list  of  objects  with  conflicting  versions  (see Section 3.H), rather than a single object.
texts.text: To read and write replicated data, Dynamo uses a protocol similar  to  those  used  in  quorum  systems.  This  protocol  has two parameters R / W -the minimal number of nodes that must participate  in  a  successful read/write operation  respectively. When a coordinator receives  a  write  operation,  it  writes  the data  locally  and  then  sends  a  write  request  to  the  other  N-1 replica nodes. If at least W-1 nodes respond, the operation is considered successful and the coordinator informs the client. When  a  read  operation  is  received,  the  coordinator  sends  a read  request  to  the  N-1  nodes,  and  if  at  least  R-1  nodes respond, it returns the result to the client. If different objects are  received  from  different  nodes,  then  coordinator  sends  to the  client  a  list  of  objects  with  conflicting  versions  (see Section 3.H), rather than a single object.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Tablet servers in BigTable handle read and write requests for  the  tablets  that  they  serve.    Tablet  data  operations  are performed  as  illustrated  in  Fig.  1.  When  a  write  operation arrives at a tablet server,  it is written to the commit log (this log  is  used  to  recover  the  tablet  in  case  of  crash).  After  the write  has  been  committed,  its  content  is  inserted  into  the memtable -an in-memory sorted buffer. When the memtable size reaches a certain threshold, the memtable is frozen, a new memtable is created, and the frozen memtable is converted to an  SSTable  and  is  written  to  GFS.  From  time  to  time  all SSTables  are  merged  to  exactly  one  SSTable.  When  a  read operation arrives at a tablet server, it is executed on a merged view of the sequence of SSTables and the memtable. Since the SSTables  and  the  memtable  are  sorted  data  structures,  the merge can be performed efficiently. To reduce the number of disk  accesses  required  to  read  all  SSTables  for  each  read operation, BigTable uses Bloom filters. Bloom filters are kept in the main memory and allow checking whether the specific SSTable  might  contain  any  data  for  a  specified  row/column pair.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Concurrency  control  deals  with  the  issues  involved  with allowing multiple  clients  access  shared  objects  concurrently. Not surprisingly, the implementation of concurrency control is different in each system.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Dynamo  is  designed  as  an  eventually  consistent  system. Write operations return before all replica nodes have applied the  update.  As  a  consequence,  read  operations  may  return different  versions  of  the  same  object.  Dynamo's  clients  are designed to  handle  such  inconsistencies.  For  example,  if  the "shopping cart" application receives different versions of the user's  shopping  cart,  it  can  resolve  the  conflict,  by  updating the cart to be the merge view of all the conflicting carts. Using this reconciliation mechanism, items which were added to the cart  are  never  lost.  However,  deleted  items  can  reappear.  In

texts.orig: BigTable guaranties that read and write operations under a single  row  key  are atomic. As  shown  in  Fig. 1, write operations access the tablet log and the memtable, while read operations  access  the  memtable  and  the  SSTables.  Thus  the only data structure that is accessed by both reads and writes is the memtable. To allow reads and writes of the memtable to proceed in parallel, BigTable makes each memtable row copyon-write.  This  means  that  each  time  a  memtable  row  is updated a new copy of the row is created. With this copy-onwrite  approach,  BigTable  can  support  concurrent  read  and write operations without using heavy synchronization mechanisms as locks.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: A. Riak (http://basho.com/riak)
texts.text: A. Riak (http://basho.com/riak)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Riak is a Dynamo-like distributed key-value data storage system which was built by Basho. It was written in Erlang and was  open-sourced  in  2009.  Riak  uses  most  of  the  Dynamo techniques and can be considered as a direct implementation of  [2].  However  Riak  has  its  own  features  as  well.  One  of them  is  a  "links"  feature.  Links  are  metadata  that  establish one-way  relationships  between  objects.  For  example  user  A can be linked to the set of users S, to indicate that users in S are contacts of A. Once such links are defined, queries of type "get all contacts of user A" can be executed. Actually, not only link queries are accepted by Riak but any query in the form of a function. The processing layer that handles such queries in Riak is called Riak Pipe [7].

It  was  written  in  Java  and  was  opensourced  in  2009.  The  novelty  of  Voldemort,  compared  to Dynamo, is  its  custom  storage  engine  for  bulk-loaded  readonly  data  sets  [8]. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cassandra  is  a  distributed  storage  system,  which  was originally developed by Facebook [11]. It was written in Java and  was  open-sourced  in  2008.  Today  it  is  an  Apache  toplevel  project.  Cassandra  adopts  ideas  and  concepts  of  both Dynamo and BigTable and can be described  as  a  BigTablelike data model running on a Dynamo-like infrastructure.
texts.text: Cassandra  is  a  distributed  storage  system,  which  was originally developed by Facebook [11]. It was written in Java and  was  open-sourced  in  2008.  Today  it  is  an  Apache  toplevel  project.  Cassandra  adopts  ideas  and  concepts  of  both Dynamo and BigTable and can be described  as  a  BigTablelike data model running on a Dynamo-like infrastructure.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cassandra's  data  model  is  similar  to  BigTable's  data  model with only two extensions -super column families and a userdefined sort order. Super column family is an additional level of grouping and can be visualized as a column family within a column  family.  Applications  can  specify  the  sort  order  of columns  within  a  column  family  or  a  super  column  family. Cassandra is based on decentralized (Dynamo-like) architecture. It uses techniques similar to Dynamo's  for partitioning, replication, concurrency control and membership and  failure  detection.  However  the  read/write  operations  are implemented by using both Dynamo and BigTable approaches. Like Dynamo, Cassandra uses quorum-like protocol for reads and writes. As in BigTable, writes are first written  to  the  commit  log  and  then  to  the  in-memory  data structure (i.e. memtable). Storage layer of Cassandra is neither a  pluggable  database  as  in  Dynamo  nor  a  distributed  file system as in BigTable; it is a local file system.

texts.orig: 5. CONCLUSION
texts.text: 5. CONCLUSION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The goal of this paper is to provide an essential overview of the two, probably the most influencing, NoSQL databases -Dynamo  and  BigTable.  We  have  reviewed  and  compared these systems and have discussed open source projects which have been inspired by them.
texts.text: The goal of this paper is to provide an essential overview of the two, probably the most influencing, NoSQL databases -Dynamo  and  BigTable.  We  have  reviewed  and  compared these systems and have discussed open source projects which have been inspired by them.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To  conclude,  both  systems  are  non-relational  distributed data storage systems. Dynamo uses a decentralized architecture  with  a  key-value  data  model  and  an  eventual consistency,  while  BigTable  is  built  with  a  single  master approach, a column-oriented data model and a strong consistency.
texts.text: To  conclude,  both  systems  are  non-relational  distributed data storage systems. Dynamo uses a decentralized architecture  with  a  key-value  data  model  and  an  eventual consistency,  while  BigTable  is  built  with  a  single  master approach, a column-oriented data model and a strong consistency.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The main advantage of Dynamo over BigTable is its very high level of availability and an ability to replicate data across many  data centers world-wide. The main advantage of BigTable over Dynamo is its strong consistency and ability to store structured and ordered data.
texts.text: The main advantage of Dynamo over BigTable is its very high level of availability and an ability to replicate data across many  data centers world-wide. The main advantage of BigTable over Dynamo is its strong consistency and ability to store structured and ordered data.
